newsitem.title: USA: U.S. terms Taiwan official's visit "normal".
newsitem.headline: U.S. terms Taiwan official's visit "normal".

text.p: Taiwan's foreign minister has arrived in the United States on a private visit, a "normal element" in unofficial ties with Taiwan, the State Department said on Monday.
Apparently to placate China which has expressed concern about the visit the State Department emphasised that the foreign minister, John Chang, was not scheduled to come to Washington.

"John Chang is visiting the Western U.S. for programmes with two private organisations," Phyllis Young, a department spokeswoman, said. "We consider this to be a normal element of our unofficial relationship with Taiwan."
"The Chinese government has expressed concern over Mr. Chang's visit, and we have explained our policy," another spokeswoman added.

During his nine-day visit, Chang was to speak at a world affairs conference in Los Angeles and attend a forum in Beaver Brook, Colorado, arranged by the private American Enterprise Institute, Taiwanese officials said.

The visit comes at a sensitive time, two weeks before China resumes control over the British colony of Hong Kong at midnight on June 30. China hopes that Hong Kong's reversion will serve as a model for Taiwan's eventual reunfication with the communist-ruled mainland.

Asked if Washington feared Chang's trip could be a problem, given the heightened sensitivities surrounding Hong Kong's handover, a spokeswoman, Julie Reside, said: "No, we don't. It's the same kind of routine practice that previous Taiwanese ministers have experienced."
China accues Taiwan's leaders of manoeuvring toward a formal declaration of independence. Taiwan was the refuge of the Nationalist forces that lost the Chinese civil war in 1949.
China-U.S. relations went into a long tailspin after the Clinton administration granted a visa to Taiwanese President Lee Teng-hui to attend a Cornell University class reunion in June 1995.

U.S. officials privately drew a sharp contrast between the relatively low-ranking Chang, a government minister, and Lee, the first head of state allowed in since the United States downgraded ties with Taiwan in 1979 to establish formal relations with Beijing.

To mollify China, the United States has said it would grant visas to Taiwanese leaders such as the chief of state or head of government only on a case-by-case basis for visits that are "rare, personal and unofficial."

A State Department official said Chang's predecessor, Fred Chien, had visited the United States as a guest of private groups. "It has been our practice to allow Taiwan ministers to visit the U.S. for private activities," the official said.
